newsitem.title: FRANCE: U.S., France seek to calm Middle East over Israel.
newsitem.headline: U.S., France seek to calm Middle East over Israel.

text.p: The United States and France sought to calm Middle East tensions on Thursday after Israel announced plans to build new Jewish housing in Arab East Jerusalem, drawing worldwide condemnation.
But analysts said the decision could spark a new wave of violence over the holy city at the heart of the Arab-Israeli conflict.

Defying American and European objections and Palestinian warnings, Israeli ministers on Wednesday approved the building of a new Jewish neighbourhood of 6,500 homes on land captured in the 1967 Middle East war.
"This may be a clever diversion in domestic politics but it is an explosive provocation towards the Palestinians and all the players in the peace process," the French daily Liberation said.
Palestinians saw the move to extend a belt of Jewish housing estates around the Arab half of Jerusalem as an attempt to cement Israel's hold over the entire holy city.
The radical Islamic Resistance Movement Hamas called for the escalation of "massive resistance" in response to what it called "a declaration of war against the Arab existence in Jerusalem".

The Israeli decision, seen by many analysts as a sop to hardline Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's most hawkish supporters for last month's pullback from most of the West Bank city of Hebron, was criticised around the world.
The European Union said it deeply deplored the move and reaffirmed that "settlements in the occupied territories contravene international law and are a major obstacle to peace".

Russia called the decision "ill-considered and untimely". Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told visiting Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy it was "a negative element for the Middle East peace process".

Both the United States and France criticised the Israeli move, but in measured terms which diplomats said were designed to keep the door open for peace negotiations and discourage if possible a violent Palestinian reaction.

"The decision taken today further complicates an already complicated situation," White House spokesman David Johnson said. Palestinian President Yasser Arafat is due in Washington next month, diplomats said.

French President Jacques Chirac told Syrian Vice-President Abdel Halim Khaddam in Paris he was concerned at the development but appealed for a resumption of peace talks, frozen between the Jewish state and Damascus since Netanyahu was elected last May.
Khaddam retorted that recent Israeli initiatives showed the Jewish state did not want peace.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette is due to visit Syria, Lebanon and Israel from next Tuesday in an effort, coordinated with the United States, to encourage a revival of negotiations between the three countries.

In New York, Arab states called for an emergency Security Council meeting to demand that Israel rescind its decision to build homes for Jews in Jabal Abu Ghneim, a wooded hill between Jerusalem and Bethlehem which Israelis call Har Homa.
European commentators said the timing of the decision could scarcely have been worse, with talks on the permanent status of the West Bank and Gaza Strip due to begin within a few weeks.
They recalled that a similarly provocative decision to open a tunnel under the Arab Old City of Jerusalem near al-Aqsa Mosque led to severe bloodshed last September.

"Those who send the bulldozers run the risk of blocking the peaceful path of seeking compromise and face the danger of botching up the future," Germany's liberal Frankfurter Rundschau said in an editorial.
The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung said Israel "runs the risk that the political war of words will escalate into a bloody conflict".
